planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the soil surface in humus-rich woodland soil beneath deciduous shade; this nursery-raised cross between the white-flowered Trillium flexipes and the dark red Trillium sulcatum is grown from seed, so individual plants vary in flower color.

directions: This hybrid toadshade combines two native pedicellate trilliums, the white-flowered Trillium flexipes and the deep red Trillium sulcatum, and because nursery stock is seed-grown rather than cloned, each plant's nodding flower shows its own blend of white, cream, pink, and cinnamon-brown tones. Plants take several years to reach flowering size from seed, so the offerings typically sold are already well established and ready to settle quickly into a woodland bed. Give it the same rich, humus-laden, evenly moist soil favored by both parent species, and leave the rhizome undisturbed once planted since trilliums resent transplanting. Pair it with ferns and other spring ephemerals that can fill the gap it leaves when going dormant by midsummer.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the surface in humus-rich, moisture-retentive bottomland soil beneath deciduous cover; this selection traces to a Shelby County, Texas population near the town of Shelbyville.

directions: This selection of the slender Texas trillium traces to a population near the town of Shelbyville in Shelby County, Texas, where plants grow in moist bottomland woods and stay loosely spaced rather than forming dense clumps. Each stalk carries three grayish-green leaves patterned with olive mottling beneath narrow, mostly purple petals that open in mid-spring. Like other Trillium gracile, it prefers the same rich, seasonally moist bottomland soil of its native range and resents disturbance once established. Allow leaf litter to accumulate around the clump each fall to mimic its native forest floor.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the surface in rich, near-neutral woodland soil in dappled shade; this selection was grown from seed collected in Graham County, North Carolina.

directions: Grown from seed collected in Graham County, North Carolina, this selection of the classic great white trillium was first offered after being grown on for several years to reach flowering size. Each stalk carries a whorl of three broad green leaves topped by a single triangular white flower that opens in mid-spring and often ages toward soft pink as it fades. Like the species, it performs best in rich, humus-laden woodland soil with a near-neutral pH and dappled shade beneath deciduous trees. Avoid disturbing the rhizome once established, since Trillium grandiflorum is slow to recover from transplanting.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the surface in rich, near-neutral woodland soil in dappled shade; this selection was grown from seed collected in Monroe County, Tennessee.

directions: This nursery-propagated selection of the great white trillium grows from seed collected in Monroe County, Tennessee, and is offered as flowering-sized plants rather than wild-collected rhizomes. It shares the species' broad, three-leaved whorl and single upright white flower that opens in mid-spring, aging gradually toward pink as the bloom matures. Plant in rich, humus-rich woodland soil with a near-neutral pH beneath deciduous cover, where it will slowly naturalize over many years. As with all trilliums, leave the rhizome undisturbed once sited, since it resents being moved.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the surface in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil beneath deciduous cover; collected in 2006 near Harpersville in Shelby County, Alabama.

directions: Collected in 2006 near the town of Harpersville in Shelby County, Alabama, this population of the narrowleaf trillium grows noticeably taller than typical for the species, reaching about 10 inches, and carries especially attractive silver-patterned mottled leaves. Like other narrowleaf trilliums it produces upright maroon flowers held just above a whorl of slender leaflets in early spring before going dormant by summer. Grow in light shade in evenly moist, humus-rich woodland soil, and avoid overhead watering that can rot the shallow rhizome. It increases slowly by rhizome offsets, so allow it several years to form a substantial clump.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the surface in humus-rich, evenly moist woodland soil in light shade; derived from a solid-silver-leaved clone found in Louisiana's Caldwell Parish in 2004.

directions: Caldwell Silver traces to a single stem with completely silvered leaves found in Louisiana's Caldwell Parish in 2004, and it took roughly seventeen years to build up enough stock from that one plant to offer it as a seed strain. Plants mature at about 10 inches tall with solid silver foliage that sets it apart from the more typically mottled green-and-silver leaves of wild Trillium ludovicianum, topped by sessile, dark purple petals that can open as early as late winter in the Deep South. Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist woodland soil in light shade, and leave the clump undisturbed to bulk up over time. Its all-silver leaves make it a striking specimen even before the flowers open.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the surface in humus-rich, evenly moist woodland soil in light shade; a clonal selection from Caldwell Parish, Louisiana genetics chosen for form and flower color.

directions: Lean and Green is a clonal selection of the Louisiana trillium chosen for its well-proportioned form and unusually long, chartreuse petals, and it multiplies into a flowering clump faster than many trillium selections. Its genetics trace to a wild population in Caldwell Parish, Louisiana, and because it was released as a true clonal division rather than a seed strain, every plant is identical to the original selection. Grow it in humus-rich, consistently moist woodland soil in light shade, where its long yellow-green petals stand out against the mottled, silver-and-olive foliage typical of the species. Leave the rhizome undisturbed once planted to let the clump increase at its naturally faster pace.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the surface in rich, evenly moist, humus-laden woodland soil in light shade; this seed strain was collected near the Ouachita River in Caldwell Parish, Louisiana.

directions: This seed strain of the Louisiana trillium was collected near the Ouachita River in Caldwell Parish, Louisiana, and is offered as flowering-sized, nursery-grown seedlings rather than wild-dug rhizomes. Plants reach about 10 inches tall with silver-and-olive mottled leaves topped by narrow, deep red petals that typically open in late winter to earliest spring, among the first trilliums to bloom. Grow in rich, evenly moist, humus-laden woodland soil in light shade, and avoid disturbing the rhizome once established since the species is slow to recover from transplanting. Supplies of this strain remain limited given how recently it was introduced.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the surface in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in light to full shade; traces to a clone found near Blakely, Georgia in 2006.

directions: This selection of the spotted trillium traces to a single clone found near Blakely, Georgia, in 2006, where the population displayed darker, more heavily mottled purple foliage than is typical for the species. Foot-tall stalks carry the classic upright, deep purple, sessile flower characteristic of Trillium maculatum, opening in earliest spring ahead of most other sessile trilliums. Grow in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in light to full shade beneath deciduous trees, and leave the rhizome undisturbed once sited. Like other spotted trilliums, it slowly bulks up by rhizome offsets rather than spreading aggressively.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the surface in humus-rich, evenly moist woodland soil in light shade; preserves a rare purple-flowered color break first noticed in 2005 within the predominantly yellow-flowered South Carolina Trillium oostingii population.

directions: Camden Purple preserves an extremely rare color break found within the well-known South Carolina population of Trillium oostingii, where fewer than one percent of the predominantly yellow-flowered plants bear purple blooms instead, with no intermediate shades ever observed between the two colors. It took roughly seventeen years of growing the purple-flowered plants from seed to build up enough stock to offer this selection. Like the species, it forms dense clumps of mottled sessile leaves and is among the earlier-flowering toadshades in cultivation. Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist woodland soil in light shade, and leave it undisturbed to slowly increase.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the surface in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil with some morning sun to light shade; represents the southeasternmost known population of the species, near Roanoke Rapids in Halifax County, North Carolina.

directions: Toadshade occurs in two widely separated centers of distribution east and west of the Mississippi River, and this selection represents the southeasternmost known population, found near Roanoke Rapids in Halifax County, North Carolina. Plants are nursery-propagated from seed collected at that site and show the same upright, maroon, sessile flowers held above mottled leaves typical of Trillium sessile elsewhere in its range. Because this population grows at the warm edge of the species' distribution, it tolerates a bit more sun and heat than northern forms of the species. Grow in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil with some morning sun to light shade, and leave the rhizome undisturbed once planted.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes in fall just below the surface in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil with some morning sun to light shade; represents a northern Georgia (Decatur-area) population of a species usually associated with Florida and the Gulf Coast.

directions: This selection represents a northern Georgia population of a species usually associated with Florida and the Gulf Coast, and plants from this source emerge nearly two months later in the season than their more southern relatives. Despite the delayed emergence, the mottled leaves and upright purple flowers are essentially identical to typical Trillium underwoodii, with blooms opening in winter in mild climates. Grow in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil with a bit of morning sun to light shade, and mark the planting site since the foliage goes fully dormant by summer. It is best sited among other early-blooming woodland natives that can take over seasonal interest once it disappears below ground.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average garden soil from slightly acidic to slightly alkaline in part sun to shade; a recently recognized triploid segregate of the Dryopteris affinis complex, centered in Central European populations.

directions: Dryopteris cambrensis is a triploid segregate of the familiar golden-scaled male fern complex, only recently recognized as a distinct species and centered on populations from Poland and the Czech Republic despite its Latin name. It forms a solitary, elegant evergreen clump of fronds that can reach 30 inches tall and 3 feet across, holding up well through hot, humid summers that can stress other European wood ferns. New croziers emerge clothed in the warm rust-colored scales typical of the affinis group before unfurling into broad, finely cut fronds. It tolerates an unusually wide soil pH range, from slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, making it adaptable to garden soils that would challenge more particular fern species.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade; an easy-care East Asian evergreen clumping wood fern that is notably deer and rabbit resistant.

directions: Dryopteris commixta is an easy-care East Asian wood fern whose new croziers emerge on wiry black stems in spring, each one tipped with dark, curled growth that gardeners often compare to a pair of insect antennae before it unfurls. Mature fronds are dark green, glossy, and held upright to about two feet, with a tuft of blackish, fur-like scaling persisting at the base of each frond stem. It stays evergreen in milder winters, resists deer and rabbit browsing, and is vigorous enough that well-established clumps a decade old remain full and healthy. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade, where its glossy dark foliage makes a strong textural contrast against golden- or silver-leaved companions.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade; a lesser-known, deer-resistant relative of the popular autumn fern with shorter, broader fronds.

directions: Dryopteris nipponensis is a lesser-known relative of the popular autumn fern, forming an evergreen, deer-resistant clump roughly 2 feet tall and 3 feet across with fronds that are shorter and noticeably broader than those of Dryopteris erythrosora. The refined texture of its foliage has made it a favorite among visitors to the display gardens where it is grown, even though it remains uncommon in general nursery trade. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade, where it holds its form and color through most of the winter in milder climates. Give it the same general care as autumn fern, dividing congested clumps in spring only occasionally since it increases at a modest pace.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to shade; native to high mountain forests of Mexico and Guatemala and more heat tolerant than most related wood ferns.

directions: Dryopteris pseudofilix-mas comes from high, moist mountain forests of Mexico and Guatemala, and unlike the familiar European male fern it does not stop producing new fronds after an initial spring flush but keeps pushing out foliage through the growing season. Semi-evergreen fronds reach about 30 inches tall and generally persist into late winter before dropping as new growth begins. It handles summer heat and humidity notably better than the related Himalayan wood fern, Dryopteris wallichiana, making it a more reliable choice for gardens outside cool mountain climates. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to shade, where its larger stature and season-long production of fresh fronds make it a standout, easy-care addition to the fern border.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade; native to subtropical evergreen forests of south-central China into Japan but considerably more cold-hardy in cultivation than its origin suggests.

directions: Dryopteris decipiens hails from subtropical evergreen forests of south-central China into Japan, yet has proven considerably more cold-hardy in cultivation than its subtropical origin would suggest. It forms a dense, low clump about a foot tall but nearly two feet wide, carrying evergreen fronds up to 15 inches long that emerge flushed with red before settling into glossy green. The contrast between the colorful spring growth and the mature dark foliage gives the clump season-long interest in the shaded border. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light to full shade, where it spreads gradually into an attractive groundcover-like patch.
